ancientNote: Home of the gods in Homer and Hesiod; Zeus wages the Titanomachy from here.
modernNote: Greece's highest mountain (2,918 m). Offerings to Zeus have been found at a sanctuary on one of its lower peaks.
confidenceNote: The mountain is certain. In poetry 'Olympus' can also mean the sky-home of the gods rather than the physical peak.

ancientNote: The Titans' stronghold in the Titanomachy, facing Olympus across the plain of Thessaly.
modernNote: A mountain range in central Greece south of the Thessalian plain.
confidenceNote: The mountain is real; its role is purely mythic, with no known cult of the Titans there.

ancientNote: Seat of Apollo's oracle, the 'navel' of the earth, where Apollo slew the serpent.
modernNote: Major archaeological site and UNESCO World Heritage Site on the slopes of Parnassus.

ancientNote: The small island that alone accepted Leto, birthplace of Apollo.
modernNote: Uninhabited island and archaeological site in the Cyclades.

ancientNote: City of King Minos, Daedalus and the Labyrinth in later myth; Homer mentions Daedalus' dancing floor there.
modernNote: Bronze Age palace excavated and partly reconstructed by Arthur Evans.
confidenceNote: The site is certain. Equating its architecture with the mythical Labyrinth is a modern suggestion, not evidence.

ancientNote: Hesiod places Zeus' hiding near Lyktos; other sources name Mount Dikte or Mount Ida.
modernNote: A cave with rich votive deposits on the Lasithi plateau; the Idaean Cave is also a major cult cave.
confidenceNote: Both caves were cult sites; which one 'is' the birthplace depends on which ancient source you follow.

ancientNote: Agamemnon's 'well-built' city, 'rich in gold', in Homer.
modernNote: Bronze Age citadel with the Lion Gate and shaft graves.

ancientNote: Priam's city, besieged for ten years by the Greeks.
modernNote: A multi-layered mound excavated since Schliemann; classical Greek Ilion stood here, and the Bronze Age levels are identified with Wilusa of Hittite texts.
confidenceNote: That Hisarlik is the place Greeks called Ilion is secure. That a war like the Iliad's was fought there is not established.

ancientNote: Athena's city, won in a contest with Poseidon.
modernNote: Capital of Greece; the Acropolis holds the Parthenon and Erechtheion.

ancientNote: Kingdom of Menelaus and Helen.
modernNote: Modern town above the ancient site. The Bronze Age centre may have been nearby, at the Menelaion or Agios Vasileios.
confidenceNote: Classical Sparta is certain; the location of a Bronze Age 'Sparta of Menelaus' is debated.

ancientNote: City of Cadmus, Semele and Oedipus; birthplace of Dionysus and Heracles.
modernNote: Modern town over a Mycenaean palace that yielded Linear B tablets.

ancientNote: One of Hera's three favourite cities in the Iliad; her great sanctuary, the Heraion, lay nearby.
modernNote: One of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in Greece.

ancientNote: Wealthy city on the Isthmus; Poseidon's Isthmian games were held nearby. In myth, Jason and Medea lived here after the voyage.
modernNote: Archaeological site with the Archaic temple of Apollo.

ancientNote: Sanctuary of Olympian Zeus and site of the Olympic Games.
modernNote: Archaeological site with the temples of Zeus and Hera.

ancientNote: Oracle of Zeus where priests interpreted the rustling of a sacred oak; Achilles prays to 'Zeus of Dodona'. Dione was worshipped beside him.
modernNote: Archaeological site in Epirus; thousands of lead question-tablets survive.

ancientNote: Where grieving Demeter rested and founded her Mysteries.
modernNote: Industrial town west of Athens around the sanctuary and Telesterion.

ancientNote: Kingdom of old Nestor, visited by Telemachus in Odyssey 3.
modernNote: The best-preserved Mycenaean palace, whose fire baked over a thousand Linear B tablets.
confidenceNote: The Bronze Age palace is certain; equating it with Homer's 'sandy Pylos' is widely accepted but rests on tradition and location.

ancientNote: Odysseus' rocky island home, described as lying 'furthest towards the dusk'.
modernNote: An Ionian island that has borne the name since antiquity.
confidenceNote: Homer's description (Od. 9.21–27) fits modern Ithaki imperfectly, which has prompted alternatives.

ancientNote: Land of King Aeetes and the Golden Fleece at the eastern edge of the world.
modernNote: Historical Colchis is a real region of western Georgia; its link with the myth's 'Aia' is a Greek identification.
confidenceNote: Earliest versions of the myth may have placed Aia in an unlocated far east; the Colchis identification is attested later.

ancientNote: A crater lake near Cumae believed to be an entrance to the underworld; Aeneas descends here, and some placed Odysseus' consultation of the dead here.
modernNote: A volcanic crater lake in the Campi Flegrei, west of Naples.
confidenceNote: Identified as an underworld entrance by ancient writers. The Odyssey's own underworld lies at the edge of Ocean and is not terrestrial.

ancientNote: The realm of the dead beneath the earth; in the Odyssey it is reached by sailing to the edge of Ocean.
modernNote: Various real caves and lakes (Avernus, Taenarum, the Acheron) were later treated as entrances.

ancientNote: The pit as far below Hades as earth is below the sky, where the Titans are imprisoned.
modernNote: A purely cosmological place.

ancientNote: Garden of the golden apples at the far western edge of the world, near Atlas, beyond Ocean.
modernNote: Ancient geographers attached the name to places in Libya and the far west, but the garden itself is mythical.

ancientNote: Calypso's island, 'the navel of the sea', far from gods and men.
modernNote: Many identifications (Gozo, Malta and others) have been proposed; none rests on ancient evidence strong enough to map.

ancientNote: Circe's island; the Odyssey places it where 'Dawn has her house and dancing floors' — in the east.
modernNote: Ancient Italians identified it with the promontory of Circeii, despite the poem's eastern setting.

ancientNote: The Thracian city Odysseus sacks first after leaving Troy.
modernNote: The Cicones were a known Thracian people; Ismarus is placed near later Maroneia.

ancientNote: Where a north wind drives Odysseus off course — the point where the voyage leaves the known world.
modernNote: South-eastern tip of the Peloponnese, notorious for storms.

ancientNote: People whose lotus fruit makes travellers forget their homecoming.
modernNote: Herodotus places Lotus-Eaters on the Libyan coast; later writers named the island of Meninx (Djerba).
confidenceNote: The poem gives nine days' storm from Malea and no fixed place; the North African identification is an ancient interpretation.

ancientNote: Where Polyphemus traps Odysseus in his cave.
modernNote: Thucydides reports the tradition that the Cyclopes were the oldest inhabitants of Sicily.
confidenceNote: Thucydides himself says he cannot say where they came from: a tradition, not a location.

ancientNote: A floating island with bronze walls where Aeolus gives Odysseus a bag of winds.
modernNote: The Lipari islands were named the Aeolian Islands in antiquity after this episode.
confidenceNote: A 'floating' island is hard to pin to any coast; the identification follows ancient naming.

ancientNote: Cannibal giants who destroy all but one of Odysseus' ships in a narrow harbour.
modernNote: Thucydides pairs them with the Cyclopes as early Sicilian peoples; other ancient and modern writers proposed Formiae or Bonifacio.

ancientNote: Singers whose song lures sailors to death; Odysseus hears it bound to the mast.
modernNote: Strabo knew the islets off the Sorrento peninsula as the Sirenussae.

ancientNote: A six-headed monster in a cliff opposite a whirlpool that swallows the sea three times a day.
modernNote: The narrow strait between Sicily and Calabria, with real strong currents.
confidenceNote: Identified with the strait since at least Thucydides; the strongest of the wanderings' identifications.

ancientName: Thrinacia, island of the Sun's cattle
ancientNote: Where Odysseus' starving crew kill the cattle of Helios and are destroyed by Zeus.
modernNote: Ancient writers equated Thrinacia with Trinacria, an old name for Sicily. No specific site.
confidenceNote: The marker sits in central Sicily to stand for the whole island, not a specific spot.

ancientNote: The idealised island of King Alcinous, where Odysseus tells his story and is carried home by a magic ship.
modernNote: Corcyreans claimed the Phaeacians as their predecessors, as Thucydides reports.
confidenceNote: A local ancient claim; the Phaeacians' near-magical society makes any identification partly symbolic.

ancientNote: No known myth; included as historical evidence for the age between palaces and poems.
modernNote: Excavated settlement and cemetery with the monumental 'heroon' building.

ancientNote: Oracle of the god Greeks called Zeus Ammon, visited by Alexander.
modernNote: Desert oasis in western Egypt with remains of the Temple of the Oracle.

ancientNote: Ptolemaic capital, home of the Serapeum and the Library.
modernNote: Egypt's second city; the Serapeum site survives in part.

ancientNote: Site of the temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva — Roman gods later equated with Zeus, Hera and Athena.
modernNote: The Capitoline Hill, with remains of the temple's foundations.
